ཕུང་པོ་དང་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་དང་ཁམས་རྣམས་ལ་རྣམ་པ་ལྔས་བཙལ་ན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། སེམས་ཅན་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་དང་། ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་མེད་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དང་གཞན་ཉིད་དུ་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བ་མ་ཡིན་པ་འཆིང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིར་བཤད་
པ། གལ་ཏེ་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་འཆིང་ན། །ཉེ་བར་ལེན་བཅས་འཆིང་མི་འགྱུར། །ཉེ་བར་ལེན་མེད་མི་འཆིང་སྟེ། །གནས་སྐབས་གང་ཞིག་འཆིང་བར་འགྱུར། །གལ་ཏེ་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་འཆིང་བ་ཡིན་པར་སེམས་ན། དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་ནི་འཆིང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། 
ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་གཉིས་སུ་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་མེད་པ་ཡང་འཆིང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་མེད་ཅིང་སྲིད་པ་མེད་པ་ལ་གང་གིས་ཀྱང་འཆིང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་འོ་ན་ད་གནས་སྐབས་
གསུམ་པ་གང་ཞིག་འཆིང་བར་འགྱུར་བར་རྟོག །ཡང་གཞན་ཡང་། གལ་ཏེ་བཅིངས་པའི་སྔ་རོལ་ན། །འཆིང་བ་ཡོད་ན་འཆིང་ལ་རག །དེ་ཡང་མེད་དེ་ལྷག་མ་ནི། །སོང་དང་མ་སོང་བགོམ་པས་བསྟན། །གལ་ཏེ་བཅིངས་པའི་དངོས་པོའི་སྔ་རོལ་ན་འཆིང་བ་ཡོད་ན་ནི་དེས་
དེ་འཆིང་ལ་རག་ན་གང་གི་ཕྱིར་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་ན། འཆིང་བ་དེ་ཡང་སྔ་རོལ་ན་མེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ་འཆིང་བ་#མི་འཐད་དོ། །ལྷག་མ་ནི་སོང་བ་དང་མ་སོང་བ་དང་བགོམ་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཇི་ལྟར་སོང་བ་དང་མ་སོང་བ་དང་བགོམ་པ་དག་ལ་འགྲོ་བ་དང་འགྲོ་བའི་རྩོམ་པ་མེད་
པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་དུ། བཅིངས་པ་དང་། མ་བཅིངས་པ་དང་། འཆིང་བཞིན་པ་དག་ལ་ཡང་འཆིང་བ་དང་འཆིང་བའི་རྩོམ་པ་མེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། ཐར་པ་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །འདིར་བཤད་པ། རེ་ཞིག་བཅིངས་པ་མི་གྲོལ་ཏེ#། །མ་བཅིངས་པ་ཡང་
གྲོལ་#མི་འགྱུར། །རེ་ཞིག་བཅིངས་པ་ནི་མི་གྲོལ་ཏེ#། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། བཅིངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མ་བཅིངས་པ་ཡང་གྲོལ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། འཆིང་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གལ་ཏེ་བཅིངས་པ་གྲོལ་#བར་འགྱུར་ན། དེས་སྐྱོན་ཅིར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་

liberated. Why? Because, as before, they are not found when searched for in the five ways among the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.

Here it is asked: "Sentient beings—whether with grasping or without grasping, and who cannot be described as identical or different—are bound." Here it is explained:

If grasping were bondage,
One with grasping would not be bound.
One without grasping is not bound either;
In what state, then, would one be bound?

If you think that grasping is bondage, then one who already possesses grasping would not be bound. Why? Because it would result in the fault of having two graspings. One without grasping is also not bound. Why? Because for one without grasping and without existence, nothing can act as a bond. Therefore, in what third state do you imagine one would be bound? Furthermore:

If, prior to being bound,
Bondage existed, it would depend on the bound.
But that does not exist; the rest was shown
By the gone, the not-gone, and the being-gone.

If bondage existed prior to the bound entity, then it would depend on that entity for binding. However, upon analysis, that bondage does not exist priorly; therefore, it is not feasible for grasping to be bondage. The rest was shown by the discussion of the gone, the not-gone, and the being-gone <note>referring to the analysis of motion in Chapter 2</note>. Just as there is no motion or commencement of motion in the gone, the not-gone, and the being-gone, there is also no bondage or commencement of bondage in the bound, the unbound, and the being-bound.

Here it is asked: "Liberation exists." Here it is explained:

The bound, for a start, is not liberated;
The unbound also will not be liberated.

The bound, for a start, is not liberated. Why? Because it is already bound. The unbound also will not be liberated. Why? Because it lacks bondage. Regarding this, if you think, "If the bound were to be liberated, what fault would that entail?"...

<meta>The text continues a logical analysis regarding the existence of a self or entity within the constituents of experience.</meta>

Because if one searches for them among the <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss>, the <term>ayatanas</term> <gloss>sense sources</gloss>, and the <term>dhatus</term> <gloss>elements</gloss> through the fivefold analysis <note>a method of searching for a self as being identical to, different from, the possessor of, the container of, or the contained within the aggregates</note>, they are not found to exist.

Here, it is argued: A sentient being, whether possessed of <term>upadana</term> <gloss>appropriation or grasping</gloss> or without appropriation, would be bound by being described as either identical to or different from that appropriation.

To this, it is explained:
If appropriation itself were the bond,
Then that which already has appropriation would not be bound.
That which lacks appropriation would also not be bound.
So, in what state could one be bound?

If you think that appropriation constitutes the bond, then that which is already possessed of appropriation cannot be bound. Why is this? Because it would lead to the logical fallacy of having two appropriations <note>one that already exists and a second one that performs the act of binding</note>. That which lacks appropriation also cannot be bound. Why is this? Because for one who lacks appropriation and is without existence, there is nothing by which they could be bound. Therefore, in what third possible state do you imagine binding could occur?

Furthermore:
If the bond existed prior
To the person being bound, then it could depend on the bond.
But that bond does not exist; the remainder
Is explained by the gone, the not-gone, and the currently-going.

If the bond existed prior to the entity being bound, then that entity could depend on the bond to become bound. However, when thoroughly examined, that bond does not exist beforehand. Therefore, the notion of appropriation as a bond is not tenable. The remainder of this argument is demonstrated by the analysis of the gone, the not-gone, and the currently-going <note>referring to a classic Madhyamaka dialectic where motion is analyzed as impossible in the past, future, or present moment</note>. Just as there is no walking or beginning of walking in the gone, the not-gone, and the currently-going, there is likewise no binding or beginning of binding in the bound, the unbound, and the currently-binding.

Here, it is argued: Liberation does exist.

To this, it is explained:
First, the bound is not liberated,
And the unbound is also not liberated.

First, the bound is not liberated. Why is this? Because it is already bound. The unbound is also not liberated. Why is this? Because it lacks any bond to be liberated from. In this regard, one might think: if the bound were to be liberated, what fault would there be?

<summary>This page presents a Madhyamaka philosophical analysis of bondage and liberation, arguing that neither a grasping entity nor a non-grasping entity can logically be subject to binding or release.</summary>
<keywords>Middle Way, Madhyamaka, appropriation, upadana, bondage, liberation, skandhas, fivefold analysis</keywords>
